## 1. Methods: UCA, SAM, LMS, and QML

#### 1.1. Product Indicator Approaches (UCA) ####

# Note: On page 186, Brandt et al. (2014) claim that for the interaction model
# the term unconstrained approach (as in Marsh et al., 2004, 2006) would be 
# more adequate, but for simplicity they refer to the approach as ExUC.

method_dblcent <- function(Data = NULL, model.fit = NULL) {
  out <- modsem::modsem(model.syntax = model.fit, data = Data, method = "dblcent")
  rows <- out$coefParTable[out$coefParTable$lhs == "eta3" & out$coefParTable$op == "~", ]
  
  params <- if(nrow(rows) == 3) {
    c("eta1", "eta2", "eta1:eta2")
  } else {
    c("eta1", "eta2", "eta1:eta2", "eta1:eta1", "eta2:eta2")
  }
  
  RESULTS <- list(
    "Estimates" = setNames(rows$est, params),
    "Standard Errors" = setNames(rows$se, params),
    "P-values" = setNames(rows$pvalue, params),
    "CI_lower" = setNames(rows$ci.lower, params),
    "CI_upper" = setNames(rows$ci.upper, params)
  )
  
  RESULTS
}

#### 1.2 Structural-After-Measurement (SAM) Approach ####

method_sam <- function(Data = NULL, estimator = "ML",
                       joint = FALSE, add.attr = FALSE, 
                       model.fit = NULL,
                       mm.list = NULL) {
  out <- lavaan::sam(model.fit, data = Data, se = "local",
                     mm.args = list(estimator = estimator),
                     mm.list = mm.list)
  
  # parameter estimates 
  est_table <- parameterEstimates(out)
  coefs <- est_table[est_table$lhs == "eta3" & est_table$op == "~", ]
  
  params <- if(nrow(coefs) == 3) {
    c("eta1", "eta2", "eta1:eta2")
  } else {
    c("eta1", "eta2", "eta1:eta2", "eta1:eta1", "eta2:eta2")
  }
  
  rows <- est_table$lhs == "eta3" & est_table$op == "~" & est_table$rhs %in% params
  
  ests <- setNames(est_table$est[rows], est_table$rhs[rows])
  ses  <- setNames(est_table$se[rows], est_table$rhs[rows])
  pval <- setNames(est_table$pvalue[rows], est_table$rhs[rows])
  ci_lower <- setNames(est_table$ci.lower[rows], est_table$rhs[rows])
  ci_upper <- setNames(est_table$ci.upper[rows], est_table$rhs[rows])
  
  # order according to `params`
  RESULTS <- list(
    "Estimates"        = ests[params],
    "Standard Errors"  = ses[params],
    "P-values"         = pval[params],
    "CI_lower"         = ci_lower[params],
    "CI_upper"         = ci_upper[params]
  )
  
  RESULTS
}


#### 1.3 Analytic Approaches (LMS and QML) ####

# Note: both approaches are estimated using the same function. 
# The argument "method" used in the Simulation script that calls each.

method_analytic <- function(Data = NULL, model.fit = NULL, 
                            standardized = FALSE, method = "lms") {
  out <- modsem::modsem(model.syntax = model.fit, data = Data, method = method)
  rows <- out$parTable[out$parTable$lhs == "eta3" & out$parTable$op == "~", ]
  
  # 5 parameters; we need to reorder because eta1:eta1 before eta1:eta2
  if(nrow(rows) == 5) {
    # indices of the parameters we want to swap
    eta1eta1_idx <- which(rows$rhs == "eta1:eta1")
    eta1eta2_idx <- which(rows$rhs == "eta1:eta2")
    
    # reordered index vector
    idx <- 1:nrow(rows)
    idx[eta1eta1_idx] <- eta1eta2_idx
    idx[eta1eta2_idx] <- eta1eta1_idx
    
    # swapped parameter order
    # "eta1", "eta2", "eta1:eta2", "eta1:eta1", "eta2:eta2"
    RESULTS <- list(
      "Estimates" = setNames(rows$est[idx], rows$rhs[idx]),
      "Standard Errors" = setNames(rows$std.error[idx], rows$rhs[idx]),
      "P-values" = setNames(rows$p.value[idx], rows$rhs[idx]),
      "CI_lower" = setNames(rows$ci.lower[idx], rows$rhs[idx]),
      "CI_upper" = setNames(rows$ci.upper[idx], rows$rhs[idx])
    )
  } else {
    # 3 parameters, keep as it was before:
    # "eta1", "eta2", "eta1:eta2"
    RESULTS <- list(
      "Estimates" = setNames(rows$est, rows$rhs),
      "Standard Errors" = setNames(rows$std.error, rows$rhs),
      "P-values" = setNames(rows$p.value, rows$rhs),
      "CI_lower" = setNames(rows$ci.lower, rows$rhs),
      "CI_upper" = setNames(rows$ci.upper, rows$rhs)
    )
  }
  
  RESULTS
}

# The general SEM framework 

*Notation*. Bold lowercase symbols (i.e., $\boldsymbol{\eta}$, $\boldsymbol{\nu}$, $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$) denote column vectors, whereas bold uppercase symbols (i.e., $\mathbf{B}$, $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$, $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$, $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$) denote matrices. Non-bold are scalars. Let $m$ be the number of latent variables and $p$ the number of observed indicators. We work with a SEM that contains both a structural and a measurement part, using LISREL all-$y$ notation. We assume the observed data are complete and continuous. Because the literature on DBLCENT, LMS, and QML traditionally uses standard LISREL notation, we will differentiate between $\eta_x$ and $\eta_y$ when referring to those methods; for LSAM this distinction is not needed. 

For the structural model, we have 

\begin{equation}\label{eq:structural}
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\eta} = \boldsymbol{\alpha} + \mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\eta} + \boldsymbol{\zeta},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

where $\boldsymbol{\eta}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the latent vector, $\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ the intercepts, and $\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ with $\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{B})=\mathbf{0}$ and $(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{B})$ invertible. The disturbance $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})=\mathbf{0}$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})=\boldsymbol{\Psi}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$. Note that no distributional form is assumed here. Thus, given $\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})=\mathbf{0}$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})=\boldsymbol{\Psi}$, we obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}) &= (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\alpha} \\
\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\eta}) &= (\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\big((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}\big)^{\top}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For the measurement model, we relate indicators to the latent variables as

\begin{equation}\label{eq:measurement}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{y} = \boldsymbol{\nu} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\eta} + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

where $\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ is the indicator vector, $\boldsymbol{\nu}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ the intercepts, $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times m}$ the loadings, and $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ the measurement errors with $\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=\mathbf{0}$, $\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=\boldsymbol{\Theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$, 
$\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^\top)=\mathbf{0}$, and $\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\boldsymbol{\zeta}^\top)=\mathbf{0}$. The model-implied mean vector and covariance matrix of $\mathbf{y}$ are

\[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\mu} &= \boldsymbol{\nu} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\,\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}) \\
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} &= \mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{y}) = \boldsymbol{\Lambda}\,\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\eta})\,\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\top} + \boldsymbol{\Theta}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Substituting the structural moments yields

\begin{equation}\label{eq:moments}
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\mu} &= \boldsymbol{\nu} + \boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\alpha} \\
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} &= \boldsymbol{\Lambda}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Psi}(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{B})^{-\top}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^{\top} + \boldsymbol{\Theta}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Traditionally, we collect the free parameters across the structural part $(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\mathbf{B},\boldsymbol{\Psi})$ and the measurement part $(\boldsymbol{\nu},\boldsymbol{\Lambda},\boldsymbol{\Theta})$ into $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ (length $T$). Given i.i.d. data vectors $\mathcal{Y}=\{\mathbf{y}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{y}_N\}$, we estimate $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ by minimizing the discrepancy between observed and model-implied moments. Thus, estimation proceeds as a joint ('system-wide') approach where all parameters are estimated jointly.

Crucially, for estimation choices where distributional assumptions are added, normality enters only with likelihood-based estimators such as normal-theory ML (or GLS). In that case, we assume $\boldsymbol{\zeta}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Psi})$ and $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Theta})$, which implies

\[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\eta}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\alpha},\;(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Psi}\big((\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{B})^{-1}\big)^{\top}\right)
\end{aligned}
\]

and, consequently,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{y}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\right),
\end{aligned}
\]

with $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ as above in \eqref{eq:moments}.

# Interactions Approaches

## LSAM

The central idea of LSAM is to use the estimated measurement-model parameters with observed moments to construct the latent mean $\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta})$ and covariance $\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\eta})$ [@rosseel_loh_2024]. For that, we start from the measurement model in \eqref{eq:measurement} and solve for $\eta$:

\[
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\eta} = \mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol{\nu} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}.
\]

As in @rosseel_loh_2024, we let $\mathbf{M}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}$ be a mapping matrix with $\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\mathbf{I}_m$. Multiplying both sides by $\mathbf{M}$ gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\eta} = \mathbf{M}\,[\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol{\nu} - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}] = \underbrace{\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol{\nu})}_{\mathbf{f}}\;-\;\underbrace{\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_{\mathbf{r}},
\end{aligned}
\]

so defining $\mathbf{f}=\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol{\nu})=\boldsymbol{\eta}+\mathbf{r}$ with $\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$, $\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{r})=\mathbf{0}$, and $\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{r})=\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\Theta}\mathbf{M}^{\top}$. Then

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}) &= \mathbf{M}\,[\mathbb{E}(\mathbf{y})-\boldsymbol{\nu}],\\
\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\eta}) &= \mathbf{M}\,[\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{y})-\boldsymbol{\Theta}]\,\mathbf{M}^{\top}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If the SEM model contained no interactions or quadratic terms, one could proceed naturally as in @rosseel_loh_2024, but for two-way interactions and quadratic terms we need second moments. Hence, @rosseel_etall_2025 proposed an expression for $\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}\otimes\boldsymbol{\eta})$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\eta}\otimes\boldsymbol{\eta})$ without assuming normality for the latent variables:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}\otimes\boldsymbol{\eta}) 
= \operatorname{vec}\!\big[\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\eta})\big]+\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta})\otimes \mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}).
\end{aligned}
\]

Let $\mathbf{K}_m\in\mathbb{R}^{m^2\times m^2}$ be the commutation matrix. Using $\mathbf{f}=\boldsymbol{\eta}+\mathbf{r}$ with $\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{r})=\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\Theta}\mathbf{M}^{\top}$, an approximation for the variance of the Kronecker product is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\eta}\otimes\boldsymbol{\eta})
\;\approx\; \mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{f}\otimes\mathbf{f})
-\Big[\,\mathbf{Q}+\mathbf{K}_m\mathbf{Q}+\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}_m^{\top}+\mathbf{K}_m\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}_m^{\top}
+\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{22}^{*(NT)}(\mathbf{r})\,\Big],
\end{aligned}
\]

where

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{Q} = \mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\eta})\otimes \mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{r})
+ \big(\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta})\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta})^{\top}\big)\otimes \mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{r}),
\end{aligned}
\]

and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{22}^{*(NT)}(\mathbf{r})$ is the correction term built from $\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{r})$.

Importantly, to capture covariances between first- and second-order terms, we augment the following:

\[
\boldsymbol{\eta}^*=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ \boldsymbol{\eta}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m+1},\quad
\mathbf{f}^*=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ \mathbf{f}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m+1},\quad
\mathbf{r}^*=\begin{bmatrix}0\\ \mathbf{r}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{m+1},
\]

and use

\[
\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^*\otimes \boldsymbol{\eta}^*)=\operatorname{vec}\!\big[\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^*)\big]+\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^*)\otimes\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^*),
\]

\[
\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^*\otimes \boldsymbol{\eta}^*) \approx 
\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{f}^*\otimes \mathbf{f}^*) 
-\Big[\mathbf{Q}^*+\mathbf{K}_{m+1}\mathbf{Q}^*+\mathbf{Q}^*\mathbf{K}_{m+1}^{\top}
+\mathbf{K}_{m+1}\mathbf{Q}^*\mathbf{K}_{m+1}^{\top}
+\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{22}^{*(NT)}(\mathbf{r}^*)\Big],
\]

with

\[
\mathbf{Q}^*=\mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^*)\otimes \mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{r}^*)
+\big(\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^*)\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}^*)^{\top}\big)\otimes \mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{r}^*).
\]

Therefore, one can use the estimates of these augment summary statistics for a regression model in the second setp of the estimation procedure. 

**Assumptions and Performance**. Similar to the 2SMM approach, in the first stage, LSAM inherits the CFA measurement model assumptions. Distributional assumptions in the CFA stage depend on the estimator used. Concerning the second stage, specifically for the second-order corrections, the LSAM assumes only $\mathbf{r}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\Theta}\mathbf{M}^\top)$. No distributional assumptions are imposed on the latent predictors $\boldsymbol{\eta}$. For the local two-step standard errors, a sandwich formula for "robust" standard errors is used (future work will elaborate the derivations for it in contrast to the 2SMM). Importantly, for the LSAM, alpha correction may be applied, which introduces some bias in order to obtain lower variance (see Rosseel et al.). Reliability reduces $\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{r})$ and therefore shrinks the measurement-error corrections, leading to smaller sampling variance/MSE. Lastly, variability may increase only for heavy-tailed/skewed cases as higher-order moments inflate $\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf{f}\otimes\mathbf{f})$.

With respect to previous simulation studies, LSAM should in principle perform similarly to the 2SMM as observed in @rosseel_etall_2025. Indeed, the results show that bias for both approaches was small under normal and non-normal conditions. Moreover, the variance of the point estimates as well as the mean squared error were also closely related. Moreover, the general findings from previous simulation studies investigated the 2SMM approach (Brandt et al. 2014; Wall & Amemiya, 2003) should extend to the LSAM.

## Distribution Analytic (LMS and QML)

Let $k$ be the number of endogenous latents and $n_x$ the number of exogenous latent predictors; set $m=k+n_x$. Stack
$\boldsymbol{\eta}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\eta}_y\\ \boldsymbol{\eta}_x\end{bmatrix}$ with
$\boldsymbol{\eta}_y\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ and $\boldsymbol{\eta}_x\in\mathbb{R}^{n_x}$, and collect the $p$ indicators in $\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$. The measurement model is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{y}=\boldsymbol{\nu}+\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\boldsymbol{\eta}+\boldsymbol{\epsilon},
\end{aligned}
\]

where $\boldsymbol{\nu}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$, $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times m}$,
$\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$, and $\boldsymbol{\Theta}=\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$.

Use strict all-$y$ notation for the structural model,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\eta}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}+\mathbf{B}\boldsymbol{\eta}+\boldsymbol{\zeta},
\end{aligned}
\]

with block structure

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{B}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{B}_{yy}&\mathbf{B}_{yx}\\ \mathbf{0}&\mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix},\quad
\boldsymbol{\alpha}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\alpha}_y\\ \mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix},\quad
\boldsymbol{\zeta}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\zeta}_y\\ \boldsymbol{\zeta}_x\end{bmatrix},\quad
\boldsymbol{\Psi}=\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol{\zeta})=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{yy}&\mathbf{0}\\ \mathbf{0}&\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{xx}\end{bmatrix},
\end{aligned}
\]

where $\mathbf{B}_{yy}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}$, $\mathbf{B}_{yx}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n_x}$,
$\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{yy}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}$, and $\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{xx}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_x\times n_x}$. For identification, fix $\mathbb{E}(\boldsymbol{\eta}_x)=\mathbf{0}$.

To include nonlinear effects (LPT) without selectors, write the endogenous block explicitly:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\eta}_y
=\boldsymbol{\alpha}_y+\mathbf{B}_{yy}\boldsymbol{\eta}_y+\mathbf{B}_{yx}\boldsymbol{\eta}_x
+\big(\mathbf{I}_k\otimes \boldsymbol{\eta}_x^{\!\top}\big)\boldsymbol{\Omega}\,\boldsymbol{\eta}_x
+\big(\mathbf{I}_k\otimes \boldsymbol{\eta}_x^{\!\top}\big)\boldsymbol{\Xi}\,\boldsymbol{\eta}_y
+\boldsymbol{\zeta}_y,
\end{aligned}
\]

with $\mathbf{I}_k$ the $k\times k$ identity and $\otimes$ the Kronecker product, and

\[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Omega}_1\\ \vdots\\ \boldsymbol{\Omega}_k\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{k n_x\times n_x},\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Xi}=\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\Xi}_1\\ \vdots\\ \boldsymbol{\Xi}_k\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{k n_x\times k},
\]

where each $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n_x\times n_x}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Xi}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n_x\times k}$. A reduced-form rearrangement is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{C}^{-1}=\Big(\mathbf{I}_k-\mathbf{B}_{yy}-(\mathbf{I}_k\otimes \boldsymbol{\eta}_x^{\!\top})\boldsymbol{\Xi}\Big)^{-1},\qquad
\boldsymbol{\eta}_y=\mathbf{C}^{-1}\!\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_y+\mathbf{B}_{yx}\boldsymbol{\eta}_x+(\mathbf{I}_k\otimes \boldsymbol{\eta}_x^{\!\top})\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{\eta}_x+\boldsymbol{\zeta}_y\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

Special case ($k=1$, $n_x=2$, $\mathbf{B}_{yy}=\mathbf{0}$, $\boldsymbol{\Xi}=\mathbf{0}$). With $\boldsymbol{\eta}_x=(\eta_{x1},\eta_{x2})^\top$,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\eta_y=\alpha_y+\mathbf{B}_{yx}\boldsymbol{\eta}_x+\boldsymbol{\eta}_x^{\!\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}_1\boldsymbol{\eta}_x+\zeta_y,
\end{aligned}
\]

where $\mathbf{B}_{yx}=(\gamma_1,\gamma_2)$ and

\[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_1=\begin{bmatrix}\beta_1 & \tfrac{\omega}{2}\\[2pt] \tfrac{\omega}{2} & \beta_2\end{bmatrix}
\ \Rightarrow\
\boldsymbol{\eta}_x^{\!\top}\boldsymbol{\Omega}_1\boldsymbol{\eta}_x=\beta_1\eta_{x1}^2+\omega\,\eta_{x1}\eta_{x2}+\beta_2\eta_{x2}^2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Distributional assumptions for LMS/QML (mutually independent):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\eta}_x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{xx}),\qquad
\boldsymbol{\zeta}_y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{yy}),\qquad
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Theta}).
\end{aligned}
\]

LMS sketch: let $\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{xx}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{\top}$ (Cholesky), write $\boldsymbol{\eta}_x=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}$ with $\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{n_x})$, and integrate the nonlinear components to obtain a Hermite–Gauss quadrature approximation

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf{y})\approx \sum_{j=1}^{M}\pi_j\,\varphi\!\big(\mathbf{y}\mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_j,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\big).
\end{aligned}
\]

QML sketch: apply a fixed full-rank linear transform to $\mathbf{y}$ so exactly one component is non-normal while the others are (conditionally) normal; specify the implied mean/variance under the same LPT structure and maximize a quasi-log-likelihood with robust (sandwich) SEs.

**Assumptions and Performance**. The LMS assumes jointly normal latent predictors and structural disturbance, i.e., $\boldsymbol{\eta}_x\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Psi}{xx})$, $\zeta_y\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Psi}_{yy})$, with independent normal measurement errors $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\boldsymbol{\Theta})$. Hence, under these conditions we obtain estimates that are consistent, asymptotically unbiased, efficient, and normal. Indeed, previous simulation results show that the LMS produced unbiased results under the condition of normally distributed $\boldsymbol{\eta}_x$. Recently, however, @lonati_etall_2025 also manipulated the distribution for the structural disturbance and measurement errors. In that case, the results showed that the distribution for the measurement error did not have much negative impact. 

Moreover, the QML applies a linear transform and models an approximating density that requires only (approximate) conditional normality of the latent criterion given the predictors. Thus, it does not require $\boldsymbol{\eta}_x$ to be normal. Under normal data, QML can be slightly less efficient than LMS. Under nonnormal latent predictors, QML is typically more robust than LMS, showing lower bias and smaller or comparable MSE, and it scales well as the number of nonlinear terms grows. Reliability affects QML through the indicator error variance in the same way.
